title: App Service vs Functions vs Container Apps
description: Compare Azure App Service, Azure Functions, and Azure Container Apps to choose the right hosting model for your workload.

data.text: Azure offers several compute services that can run your code. The three most common for application hosting are App Service, Functions, and Container Apps. Each has a sweet spot, and choosing the wrong one can lead to higher costs or unnecessary complexity.

data.title: App Service vs Functions vs Container Apps

cards.title: App Service
cards.description: Managed platform for always-on web apps and APIs.
pros: Supports many runtimes out of the box
Easy deployment with ZIP, Git, or GitHub Actions
cons: Always-on instances cost money even when idle

cards.title: Azure Functions
cards.description: Serverless functions that run on demand.
pros: Pay only while code is executing
Scales from zero to thousands automatically
Many built-in triggers (HTTP, timer, queue, blob)
cons: Execution time limits on the Consumption plan

cards.title: Azure Container Apps
pros: Runs Docker containers without managing Kubernetes
Built-in service mesh and Dapr support
Scales based on traffic or events
cons: More complex networking than App Service
Overkill for a single simple web app

rows: Background job triggered by a queue
Runs only when needed, scales automatically
Blob trigger reacts instantly to new files
Use your existing containers with managed scaling
Service mesh and ingress built in
Fastest to deploy, lowest initial cost

terms.definition: A setting that keeps an App Service app loaded and ready to serve requests without cold starts.
A Functions pricing model where you pay only for execution time and memory used.
A serverless container platform that runs Docker images without managing Kubernetes clusters.
An event that starts a Functions execution, such as an HTTP request, timer, or queue message.

data.caption: Start with the workload shape: continuous web traffic points to App Service, event-driven work to Functions, and containerized microservices to Container Apps.

data.title: Three deployments, three models
data.content: Each command assumes an existing resource group. Notice how much less configuration App Service and Functions need compared with a container app.
data.code:
# App Service: code deployed to a managed plan
az webapp create \
  --name demo-web-$RANDOM \
  --resource-group rg-demo \
  --plan plan-demo \
  --runtime "DOTNETCORE:8.0"

# Functions: code deployed to a consumption plan
az functionapp create \
  --name demo-fn-$RANDOM \
  --resource-group rg-demo \
  --consumption-plan-location westeurope \
  --runtime dotnet-isolated \
  --runtime-version 8 \
  --functions-version 4 \
  --storage-account demofnstorage$RANDOM

# Container Apps: an image deployed to a serverless container environment
az containerapp env create \
  --name env-demo \
  --resource-group rg-demo \
  --location westeurope

az containerapp create \
  --name demo-api \
  --resource-group rg-demo \
  --environment env-demo \
  --image myregistry.azurecr.io/demo-api:1.0 \
  --target-port 8080 \
  --ingress external \
  --min-replicas 0 \
  --max-replicas 10

data.title: Interview angle: the trade-off is control vs operational burden
data.text: App Service is the lowest-effort option for a long-running web app or API and has no cold start. Functions scales to zero and charges per execution, but a consumption-plan function can cold-start and has a execution timeout. Container Apps gives you containers, KEDA-based scaling, and Dapr without exposing Kubernetes, but you own the image and the environment. None is universally better; the right answer depends on traffic shape, team skills, and how much platform work you want.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: App Service is the default choice for web apps and APIs that run continuously.
Functions excel at event-driven, sporadic, or scheduled workloads.
Container Apps are best when your app already runs in Docker or when you need microservices.
You can mix them: a web app on App Service, background jobs on Functions, and microservices on Container Apps.
data.takeaway: There is no single best choice — match the service to the workload.
